france24fr.title: Zverev à Roland-Garros : le sacre qui met les médias face à leurs contradictions

nzz.description: Seit April gilt eine Waffenruhe zwischen Israel und Iran. Doch am Montag griffen sich die beiden Staaten wieder gegenseitig an. Die Folgen des Konflikts sind weltweit spürbar. Die neuesten Entwicklungen im Live-Ticker.

nzz.title: DIE NEUESTEN ENTWICKLUNGEN - Waffenruhe im Gazastreifen: Italien ermittelt gegen Israels rechtsextremen Polizeiminister Itamar Ben-Gvir
nzz.description: Die Waffenruhe zwischen Israel und der Hamas ist brüchig. Bis zu einem nachhaltigen Frieden im Nahen Osten ist es ein weiter Weg. Die wichtigsten Fragen und Antworten.

nzz.title: DIE NEUESTEN ENTWICKLUNGEN - Trumps zweite Amtszeit: Bundesrichter erklärt Trumps 100 000-Dollar-Visa-Gebühr für hochqualifizierte Arbeitskräfte für unzulässig
nzz.description: Donald Trump regiert zum zweiten Mal als amerikanischer Präsident – mit weitreichenden innen- und aussenpolitischen Folgen. Die neuesten Entwicklungen im Überblick.

nzz.title: KURZMELDUNGEN - Schweiz: Noch keine Einigung über die Finanzierung der 13. AHV-Rente
Ein Trauerspiel ist zu Ende: Deutschland und Frankreich beerdigen ihr gemeinsames Kampfflugzeugprojekt FCAS
nzz.description: Die deutsche Regierung zog am Montag die Reissleine, nachdem sich die beteiligten Rüstungsunternehmen nicht auf die Aufteilung der jeweiligen Anteile hatten einigen können. Für Europas Rüstung ist das ein Schlag, aber keine Katastrophe. Es gibt längst Alternativen.

nzz.title: DER ANDERE BLICK - Aussenminister Wadephul hat nichts aus der Niederlage in New York gelernt
nzz.description: Deutschland insistiert auf einem Sitz im Uno-Sicherheitsrat. Das zeigt ein tieferes Problem: Berlin hält seinen Machtanspruch weiterhin für selbstverständlich. Viele andere Staaten tun das längst nicht mehr.

nzz.title: Tech-Zweifel und der Krieg in Iran drücken auf die Börsenstimmung
nzz.description: Der Ausverkauf bei den Technologietiteln verunsichert die Märkte. Anleger fragen sich, ob es nur eine notwendige Korrektur der vorangegangenen Euphorie ist – oder ob nun Zurückhaltung angebracht ist.

nzz.title: Nach gegenseitigem Beschuss verkünden Israel und Iran, dass sie ihre Angriffe vorerst einstellen
nzz.description: Nach einem israelischen Angriff auf die libanesische Hauptstadt Beirut feuerte Teheran ballistische Raketen auf Israel ab. Der jüdische Staat antwortete mit Bombardierungen in Iran. Nach einem Machtwort von Donald Trump verkünden beide Seiten eine Feuerpause – doch von einer stabilen Waffenruhe kann keine Rede sein.

nzz.title: LIVE-TICKER - Krieg in der Ukraine: Tote und Verletzte nach russischen Angriffen
nzz.description: Seit über vier Jahren führt Russland Krieg gegen die Ukraine. Die wichtigsten Neuigkeiten im Überblick.

nzz.title: Der Bund schreibt den Schulen drei Lektionen Sportunterricht pro Woche vor. Damit könnte bald Schluss sein
nzz.description: Vertreter von Bund und Kantonen fordern das Ende der nationalen Schulsportpflicht.

nzz.title: «Die wollen Transjugendliche vernichten!» – «Die SVP hat alle Menschen gern!»
nzz.description: Im Zürcher Kantonsrat gab es am Montag kein Halten mehr. Eine Vorlage zur Gleichstellung von queeren Menschen verführte links und rechts zu abstrusen Argumenten.

nzz.title: «Gibt es weitere Fälle wie Lyhanna?» – Der Mord an einem elfjährigen Mädchen in Frankreich wird zur Justizaffäre
nzz.description: In Südfrankreich wurde vergangene Woche die Leiche der elfjährigen Lyhanna gefunden. Gegen ihren mutmasslichen Mörder lagen bereits mehrere Strafanzeigen wegen Vergewaltigungen vor. Nun lässt die Regierung rund 70 000 Fälle überprüfen, die Straftaten gegen Minderjährige betreffen.

nzz.title: KOMMENTAR - Irans Regime interessiert sich nicht für Libanon – mit seinen Raketen auf Israel testet es Trump
nzz.description: Das Regime versucht, angebliche Differenzen zwischen Trump und Netanyahu auszunutzen und damit Konzessionen am Verhandlungstisch zu erzwingen. Washington sollte hart bleiben.

nzz.title: Der Papst im spanischen Parlament: Ein Appell an Gemeinsamkeit und Humanismus
nzz.description: Leo XIV. hält in Madrid eine historische Rede und wird allseits stürmisch gefeiert. Dabei hatte er nicht nur Komplimente mitgebracht – wie vor allem die Rechtspopulisten erfahren mussten.

nzz.title: Doch keine Millionen für Choupette: Lagerfelds berühmte Katze erhält nichts aus dem Nachlass
nzz.description: Die Katze Choupette war die grosse Liebe des Modeschöpfers Karl Lagerfeld.  Nach seinem Tod hielt sich jahrelang die Legende, das berühmte Haustier werde zur Millionenerbin. Nun hat ein Gericht entschieden: Choupette geht leer aus.

spiegel.title: Karim Khan: Internationaler Strafgerichtshof (IStGH) suspendiert Chefankläger - Vorwürfe sexuellen Fehlverhaltens
spiegel.description: Karim Khan lässt sein Amt als IStGH-Chefankläger bereits seit rund einem Jahr ruhen, Hintergrund sind Vorwürfe sexueller Übergriffe. Nun wurde er mit sofortiger Wirkung von seinem Dienst suspendiert.

spiegel.title: Donald Trump: Richter verbietet den USA Vergabe von 100.000-Dollar-Visa an Fachkräfte
spiegel.description: Donald Trump will US-Fachkräften auf dem heimischen Arbeitsmarkt Vorteile verschaffen. Dazu wurden Expertenvisa für Ausländer teils um das 50-fache verteuert. Doch nun sagt ein Richter: Dazu hat der US-Präsident kein Recht.

spiegel.title: Moskau gibt Kraftstoff-Probleme infolge ukrainischer Angriffe zu
spiegel.description: Seit Monaten zielt die Ukraine bei ihren Gegenangriffen auf die Ölindustrie Russlands – dort war die Ausgabe von Benzin teilweise eingeschränkt. Nun kommentiert ein Moskauer Ministerium die Lage.

spiegel.title: Omar Artan: WM-Schiedsrichter wird Einreise in die USA verweigert
spiegel.description: Er pfeift seit Jahren für die FIFA, trotzdem haben die die USA dem Schiedsrichter Omar Artan bei der Einreise die rote Karte gezeigt. Grund könnte seine Herkunft sein.

spiegel.title: Franz Müntefering über Friedrich Merz: »Lassen wir ihn doch«
spiegel.description: Noch vergangenes Jahr riet er davon ab, Friedrich Merz zu wählen, doch Franz Müntefering scheint es zu viel zu werden mit der Kanzlerkritik: Der ehemalige SPD-Chef verteidigt den CDU-Kanzler und spricht von »Hinterhältigkeit«.

spiegel.title: Konstantin Richter schreibt Sachbuch des Jahres
spiegel.description: Etwa 300 Männer, die maßgeblich über die deutsche Wirtschaft des 20. Jahrhunderts bestimmten: Für sein Sachbuch über die »Deutschland AG« ist Konstantin Richter vom Börsenverein des Deutschen Buchhandels ausgezeichnet worden.

spiegel.title: Rätsel der Woche: Welcher Bruch erfüllt die Gleichung?
spiegel.description: Bei einer reellen Zahl folgen nach dem Komma die Ziffern 123456789. Diese wiederholen sich unendlich oft. Lässt sich diese periodische Zahl als Quotient zweier ganzer Zahlen darstellen?

spiegel.title: Sohn von Mette-Marit: Marius Borg Høiby könnte vorerst freikommen
spiegel.description: Wird der Sohn der norwegischen Kronprinzessin Mette-Marit bald aus der Untersuchungshaft entlassen? Nach einem positiven Gerichtsentscheid hat die Staatsanwaltschaft Berufung eingelegt. Nun soll eine höhere Instanz urteilen.

spiegel.title: Christian Eriksen: Fußballstar erholt sich zu Hause bei seiner Familie
spiegel.description: Er wolle jetzt mit seinen Kindern Fußball spielen, schreibt Christian Eriksen in einer ersten Stellungnahme nach seinem erneuten Zusammenbruch. Der implantierte Defibrillator habe das getan, wofür er entwickelt wurde.

spiegel.title: Xi Jinping bei Kim Jong Un: Argwöhnische Nachbarn
spiegel.description: Xi Jinpings erste Auslandsreise des Jahres geht nach Pjöngjang. Bei seinem Verbündeten Kim Jong Un muss er Boden gut machen, den er an Russland verloren hat.

spiegel.title: WWDC 2026: Apple stellt Siri AI vor
spiegel.description: Zwei Jahre nachdem sie erstmals gezeigt wurde, will Apple im KI-Rennen mit einer intelligenteren Sprachassistentin aufholen. Deutsche Nutzer benötigen aber wohl noch Geduld.

spiegel.title: CDU in Sachsen-Anhalt: Landespartei geht im Wahlkampf auf Distanz zu Friedrich Merz
spiegel.description: In Ostdeutschland steht für die CDU viel auf dem Spiel, vor allem in Sachsen-Anhalt. Friedrich Merz könnte im Wahlkampf unterstützen, doch die Landespartei grenzt sich von ihrem Kanzler ab.

spiegel.title: Niedersachsen hat einen neue Slogan: »groß« und nicht mehr »klar«
spiegel.description: Niedersachsen wächst, zumindest werbetechnisch. Ein neuer Slogan, NBA-Star Dennis Schröder als Botschafter und ein Logo zum Mitpfeifen sollen das Image des Bundeslandes aufpolieren. Kostenpunkt: zehn Millionen Euro.

spiegel.title: Frankfurt am Main: Studierenden-WG bekommt 26.700 Euro zurück
spiegel.description: Dem Frankfurter Nordend steht womöglich eine größere Party bevor: Eine Wohngemeinschaft zahlte über Jahre zu viel Miete. Jetzt ist die Stadt gegen die Vermieterin vorgegangen, eine ausländische Immobiliengesellschaft.

spiegel.title: Landgericht Bremen: Jahrelange Haft und Psychiatrie für Anschlagspläne in Bremerhaven
spiegel.description: Sie wollten mit Schusswaffen und Sprengstoff möglichst viele Menschen töten. Jetzt wurde am Landgericht Bremen das Urteil gegen einen 35-Jährigen und seinen Neffen gesprochen.

spiegel.title: Stromausfall in Reutlingen könnte Brandstiftung gewesen sein
spiegel.description: Im baden-württembergischen Reutlingen ist in der Nacht in weiten Teilen der Strom ausgefallen. Noch immer sind Tausende Menschen betroffen. Nach Angaben des Energieversorgers sind mehrere Brandstellen gefunden worden.

spiegel.title: Ironman-Veranstaltung: Staatsschutz ermittelt nach mutmaßlichem Anschlag in Hamburg
spiegel.description: Auf der Ironman-Strecke in Hamburg-Kirchwerder sind etlichen Radfahrern Metallsplitter zum Verhängnis geworden, ein Sabotageakt wird vermutet. Nun schaltet sich der Staatsschutz ein.

spiegel.title: NBA-Finals: Die New York Knicks locken sogar Donald Trump an. Der ist aber nicht willkommen
spiegel.description: Den New York Knicks fehlen noch zwei Siege bis zum ersten Basketball-Triumph seit 53 Jahren. Über eine Stadt im Ausnahmezustand, Promis im Madison Square Garden und einen Besucher mit dem falschen Orange-Ton.

elpais.description: Sorprende llamarse feminista y apoyar las letras de Benito; me pregunto qué habrían dicho si hubieran sido de Julio Iglesias

elpais.description: La acusación popular solicita que se investigue a José Luis Ábalos, Koldo García y a varios empresarios señalados por el juez Calama por el rescate de la aerolínea

elpais.description: Kristen Welker rechazó las denuncias del presidente sobre fraude electoral en California. El republicano le replicó que era “estúpida o corrupta” y cortó la entrevista

elpais.description: Los dos países intercambian ataques, por primera vez en los dos meses de alto el fuego, hasta que Trump les instó a parar “inmediatamente”. “Nuestra lucha con Irán y Hezbolá aún no ha terminado”, advierte Netanyahu

elpais.description: El responsable de Seguridad Nacional del Gobierno de Benjamín Netanyahu podría enfrentar acusaciones de secuestro y tortura de ciudadanos italianos

nyt.title: Trump Previews Fall Strategy With Baseless Claims of California Vote Fraud
nyt.description: The president is using the slow count of mail ballots in California to renew his effort to cast doubt on election outcomes he doesn’t like, despite a lack of evidence of any widespread fraud.

nyt.title: Nithya Raman Secures Second LA Mayor Spot, Ending Spencer Pratt’s Run
nyt.description: Nithya Raman, a progressive Democrat who entered the mayoral race at the last minute, secured the second spot to face Mayor Karen Bass in November. Her comeback sets up an intraparty battle.

nyt.title: A Timeline of Donald Trump and Lindsey Graham’s Relationship Before the South Carolina Primary
nyt.description: Once one of President Trump’s fiercest critics, the South Carolina senator has dramatically shifted his posture over the years. Will it pay off on Tuesday in his primary?

nyt.title: Ken Paxton’s Former Defense Lawyer Endorses James Talarico
nyt.description: The lawyer, Dan Cogdell, helped save Mr. Paxton from criminal charges and an impeachment, but now he says the Texas attorney general has “lost sight of his mission.”

nyt.title: Iran and Israel Pull Back
nyt.description: Also, the N.B.A. finals arrive in New York. Here’s the latest at the end of Monday.

nyt.title: Trump Wants to Call the Shots. But in Iran, He Keeps Hitting His Limits.
nyt.description: President Trump is grappling with his own version of the sort of Middle East crisis that beset his predecessors, and that he promised to avoid.

nyt.title: Trump Visit Closes Blocks Around MSG: What to Know About Security at the Knicks Game
nyt.description: With President Trump and Mayor Zohran Mamdani set to attend Monday night’s Knicks game at Madison Square Garden, there will be strict security in Midtown Manhattan.

nyt.title: Trump Nominates Blanche for Attorney General, Setting Up Confirmation Fight
nyt.description: As acting attorney general, Todd Blanche has shown a willingness to execute the president’s maximalist demands. Whether the Senate will confirm him remains unclear.

nyt.title: Pentagon Again Revises Religious Categories for Troops
nyt.description: The Defense Department made the change after lawmakers objected to its original list, which did not include the Latter-day Saints among traditions labeled Christian.

nyt.title: Best and Worst Moments From the 2026 Tony Awards: Pink, Maya Rudolph, Cole Escola, ‘Cats’

nyt.title: Unforgettable Looks at the Tony Awards: Cole Escola, Sarah Paulson and More

nyt.title: On Broadway’s Biggest Night, ‘Saturday Night Live’ Shows Its Strength
nyt.description: The long-running sketch comedy show proved its power during the Tony Awards on Sunday, with Lorne Michaels and several former stars grabbing the spotlight.

nyt.title: Judge Throws Out Trump Administration’s Policy Imposing $100,000 Fees for H-1B Visas
nyt.description: The ruling voided “in its entirety” a policy from September requiring companies to pay $100,000 fees for H-1B visa petitions.

nyt.title: U.S. Denies Entry to World Cup Referee From Somalia

nyt.title: Governor’s Visit to ICE Detention Facility Is Strictly Limited, She Says
nyt.description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey said she was not allowed to speak with immigrants at the Delaney Hall detention center.

nyt.title: Trump Administration Seeks to Revoke U.S. Citizenship of 17 Immigrants
nyt.description: The push to denaturalize more immigrants is the latest sign that the administration is setting its sights on the legal immigration system.

nyt.title: They Spent Years on a Math Problem. Then They Were Scooped by A.I.
nyt.description: Artificial intelligence is mastering the kinds of projects that have long helped to build the careers of young mathematicians. What does that mean for their future?

nyt.title: OpenAI Files Confidentially for IPO as AI Companies Rush to Wall St.
nyt.description: The company hopes to raise billions in a highly anticipated public offering that could unlock a new generation of tech industry wealth.

npr.title: The Strait of Hormuz's 3-month closure could set a dangerous precedent, experts worry
npr.description: Has the closure of the Strait of Hormuz set a new — and dangerous — precedent for international shipping lanes?

npr.title: TikTok is driving American expats to Southeast Asia
npr.description: More Americans are rethinking where they want to live. Some are heading to Southeast Asia, drawn in part by what they're seeing on TikTok and YouTube. But those videos don't tell the whole story.

npr.title: Xi and Kim express hopes for greater ties between China and North Korea

npr.title: Israel-Iran strikes threaten truce. And, Ebola is spreading at an unprecedented rate
npr.description: Israel and Iran's recent exchange of fire is threatening the truce in the Middle East. And, the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is spreading at an unprecedented rate, officials say.

npr.title: In speech to Spanish parliament, pope demands respect for the dignity of all people
npr.description: In the first papal address to the Spanish legislature, the American pope said a "moral renewal" was necessary in legislatures and public life to ensure respect for the inherent dignity of all people.

npr.title: Chinese president visits North Korea for the first time in 7 years
npr.description: China's President Xi Jinping is in North Korea, his first trip in seven years, in a bid to reassert China's influence in the region.

npr.title: Ebola cases rise in Congo, as government revives travel restrictions
npr.description: The Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak is spreading at an unprecedented pace, Africa CDC warns.

npr.title: After trading missile fire, Israel and Iran pull back — for now
npr.description: The missile exchange marked a major escalation in the already tense region. But Israel and Iran both say they will stop attacking each other, with conditions.

npr.title: A 7.8 magnitude quake in the Philippines kills at least 32
npr.description: An offshore magnitude 7.8 earthquake rocked the southern Philippines on Monday, killing at least 32 people, injuring more than 200 others and sending a 3-foot tsunami into nearby coasts.

npr.title: Trump is remaking U.S. policy in Latin America
npr.description: Military strikes, sanctions and political pressure are becoming hallmarks of Trump's Latin America policy. NPR's Adrian Florido speaks with historian Greg Grandin about what's driving the shift.

Columnist Michael Marshall examines how archaeologists are rethinking this critical part of our history

arxiv-ai.description:

Abstract: Sudoku is a representative constraint satisfaction problem that requires global structural reasoning under strict discrete constraints. The existing works of solving Sudoku mainly focus on two dominant approaches, i.e., traditional heuristic and deep learning solver. However, they suffer from two complementary limitations: learning-based solvers lack hard correctness guarantees, while complete symbolic solvers are still prone to long-tail search.

Prediction and game-theoretic planners can suggest plausible cooperation, yet they do not return a proof that the repair respects hard rules, right-of-way, cost allocation, and ego fallback. We introduce CARVE, Certified Affordable Repair of Vetoed maneuvers

Models are not static objects: they are snapshots of time-evolving processes shaped by data, objectives, architectures, and optimization dynamics. phys-org.title: They call it 'stupid hot' for a reason: Heat muddles animal brains
phys-org.description: On a blazing hot day in South Africa, female southern pied babblers can't think straight. The medium-sized black-and-white birds are trying to get at tasty mealworms behind a see-through barrier. On cooler days, the birds can quickly figure out that all they have to do is go around the small wall of plastic. But when the mercury goes up, the birds just keep stubbornly pecking at the barrier.

phys-org.title: Cosmic bombardment may have opened Earth's crust for prebiotic chemistry
phys-org.description: Asteroids and planetesimals regularly bombarded Earth between about 4.6 billion and 3.5 billion years ago, during the Hadean and Archean eons. Because few rocks today are more than 4 billion years old, our understanding of the planet's environment during that time is limited. However, samples from the moon and its cratered surface hint at the period's rate of cosmic impacts.

phys-org.title: Super sponge can remove toxic dyes from industrial wastewater
phys-org.description: Colors brighten our lives and help define countless items we use daily—from the vibrant clothes we wear to decorative paper and packaging materials. What adds different colors to these things? Dyes, which bind themselves to the structure of the material they are coloring. For example, methylene blue (MB) is a dye used to color paper, leather products, silk and wool, and is also employed as a diagnostic agent and in the rubber and cosmetic industries. But what happens after these dyes have served

phys-org.title: How plants survive constant DNA damage: Newly identified repair protein protects growth-critical stem cells
phys-org.description: Similar to the way DNA damage can contribute to human diseases such as cancer, it can also disrupt growth, development and survival in plants. Every day, plants endure environmental stresses such as sunlight, radiation, drought and soil stress—all of which can damage their DNA. However, they cannot move away from danger. How do plants handle all that damage?

phys-org.title: Despite toxic reputation, our research shows podcasts can help men's mental health
phys-org.description: Over the last decade, podcasts have become big business, with more than a fifth of UK adults listening to podcasts each week. The format particularly resonates with men, who are more likely than women to identify as podcast fans. Men are also overrepresented as podcast hosts.

phys-org.title: River wildlife moves freely once dams are removed, but so too can invasive species
phys-org.description: Almost a quarter of all freshwater species are threatened with extinction. The removal of human-made barriers from rivers, such as dams and weirs, is a popular way to restore water flow and sediment transport to its natural state and allow fish and other aquatic wildlife to move more freely.

phys-org.title: Peptide blocks DNA breaks tied to treatment-induced leukemia, offering new prevention route
phys-org.description: Thanks to effective therapies, more and more people are now able to live with or after cancer in the long term. Consequently, the number of patients affected by the long-term effects of their treatment is also increasing. Secondary leukemias are particularly serious. These can develop when cellular stress caused by chemotherapy or radiotherapy triggers DNA breaks in specific regions of the genome. If these breaks are incorrectly repaired by the body's own repair mechanisms, detrimental rear

phys-org.title: Great mysteries of archaeology: An ancient Amazonian world revealed from the sky
phys-org.description: From the air, you see it only through the constant jolt, tilt, and shudder of the low-flying Cessna aircraft. The landscape of the Llanos de Moxos, northern Bolivia, appears as a disconnected patchwork of open grassland savannahs, forest islands, and lakes.

phys-org.title: 'The Real Scoreline' reveals the nations facing climate penalties
phys-org.description: As nations prepare to compete on the global stage this summer, researchers at the University of Reading have created a different kind of scoreboard that shows where each country really stands on climate change. The Real Scoreline compares countries using six climate indicators—including emissions, fossil fuel dependence, heat stress, projected warming and net-zero commitments—producing a single score out of a possible 99 that reveals how nations compare beyond the traditional scoreboard.

phys-org.title: Cloud-tested quantum noise model predicts superconducting qubit errors with sevenfold better accuracy
phys-org.description: Researchers from the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, and Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore have developed a practical, comprehensive noise-modeling framework for a popular class of superconducting quantum processors. Their work, published in the journal PRX Quantum, offers a sevenfold improvement in predictive accuracy over existing approaches.

phys-org.title: Satellites reveal cities' 'urban pulse,' tracking neighborhood growth in near real time
phys-org.description: For over a century, doctors have used electrocardiograms (EKGs) to render the invisible electrical activity of the human heart visible, using the pulse to diagnose disease before it becomes fatal. Now, scientists have invented a way to do the exact same thing for the places where most of humanity lives: cities.

phys-org.title: Upcoming telescopes could shed light on dark matter
phys-org.description: NASA's plans to return astronauts to the moon through the Artemis program and ultimately send humans to Mars highlight just how far space exploration has come. Yet while the moon and Mars remain compelling destinations filled with scientific mysteries, looking beyond our solar system raises even deeper questions about the universe itself.

phys-org.title: Aerosols may warm or cool the climate depending on timing, new study finds
phys-org.description: A new study from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem challenges a long-held assumption in climate science by showing that aerosols—tiny particles suspended in the atmosphere—can either warm or cool the climate, depending on the time scale considered.

phys-org.title: Chemists unlock first total synthesis of rare plant alkaloid tied to anticancer activity
phys-org.description: Plants are undeniably one of nature's most promising sources of new medicines, with monoterpenoid indole alkaloids (MIAs) being a great example. Some intricate compounds are built from multiple-linked chemical units that form highly complex three-dimensional structures. Because of their size and shape, scientists believe such oligomeric MIAs may be able to interfere with specific protein–protein interactions inside cells—a biological target that conventional small-molecule drugs often strug

phys-org.title: 5 ways data centers endanger their local communities and the country as a whole
phys-org.description: Every internet search, streamed video and AI-generated response depends on a data center somewhere. Driven by rapid growth in artificial intelligence, cloud computing and cryptocurrency, data centers have become the backbone of the modern digital economy. But though their key role is in enabling virtual and remote experiences, data centers are physical buildings in real communities around the nation and the globe.

phys-org.title: Rocket launches and reentries harm Earth's ozone layer
phys-org.description: The space industry is surging. In coming years, nearly 10,000 spacecraft are slated to launch into low-Earth orbit for a variety of purposes, such as global surveillance, space tourism, and satellite "megaconstellations" providing internet service.

phys-org.title: Magnesium transporter discovery could improve rice nutrition and taste
phys-org.description: Rice is a staple food for nearly half the global population and an important dietary source of magnesium, a mineral essential for human health, plant growth and energy metabolism. Although magnesium is known to influence grain quality and taste, the biological mechanism controlling how the mineral reaches rice grains has remained largely unknown.

phys-org.title: Brazilian breadbasket's aquifers are falling, and new satellite maps show where water stress is growing
phys-org.description: A collaboration of scientists from NASA and Brazilian research institutions has produced a detailed picture of groundwater change across Brazil. The images reveal significant declines in some of the aquifers that are critical to one of the world's largest agricultural producers.

undark.title: Promising ‘Liquid Biopsies’ May Not Be Ready for Primetime
undark.description: Multi-cancer early detection tests seek to spot cancer from a single blood draw. Enabling earlier cancer diagnoses could help save lives and limit the need for invasive interventions. But while the tests are promising, physicians have expressed doubt about routine use by low-risk and asymptomatic individuals.

undark.title: Book Review: How Radio Astronomy Made the Invisible Visible
undark.description: According to astronomer Emma Chapman’s revelatory “The Echoing Universe,” the history of radio astronomy is filled with surprises that have revealed parts of the universe that would otherwise remain hidden and invisible — DIY instruments, secrets accidentally uncovered, and persistent connections to Earth.

undark.title: Risk Aversion in Science Stifles Innovation
undark.description: Does the scientific enterprise play it too safe? C. Brandon Ogbunu argues that risk-taking in science involves a willingness to reflect on the processes and incentives of the profession — and to dramatically overhaul them if they do not work. Only then can true scientific innovation take shape.

undark.title: A Peptide, a Secretive Scientist, and a Debate Over Evidence
undark.description: Access to unapproved peptides like BPC-157 has become a cause célèbre for the MAHA movement. Undark contributing editor Sara Talpos digs into the untold history of BPC-157 and its long journey from the scientific margins to the center of a debate over U.S. drug regulation.

undark.title: Book Review: Within Our Cells, the Miracle of Constant Mutation
undark.description: Our cells are constantly mutating in a battle for the survival of the fittest that is raging inside us daily, Roxanne Khamsi writes in “Beyond Inheritance.” Many of these mutations are harmless, others are cellular deviants that lead to disease, and remarkably, some can actually self-correct.

undark.title: The Six-Week Postpartum Checkup Comes Too Late
undark.description: In the U.S., maternity care generally ends with a checkup scheduled six weeks after giving birth. This single doctor’s appointment may be efficient for billing and discharge protocols, but the timing reflects the structure of the health care system more than the reality of maternal recovery.

undark.title: Book Review:  The Case for Making Data-Driven Decisions
undark.description: In “Beyond Belief: How Evidence Shows What Really Works,” science journalist Helen Pearson profiles a group of people working in medicine and other fields who became leaders of the worldwide evidence movement, which encourages the use of data from rigorous research to direct treatments, policies, and plans.

undark.title: What the Hantavirus Story Reveals About Medical Mistrust
undark.description: The reaction to an outbreak of hantavirus on a cruise ship reveals a story about mistrust in medicine and public health. In the U.S., hantavirus disproportionately kills Native Americans. A doctor who works at a hospital on Navajo Nation writes that such mistrust always lands hardest on the most vulnerable.

undark.title: Book Review: The Mind-Boggling Science of Enormous Numbers
undark.description: In “Huge Numbers: A Story of Counting Ambitiously, From 4½ to Fish 7,” mathematician Richard Elwes shows off his love of all things numeric, and, in particular, shines a spotlight on some of the largest numbers humans have ever contemplated, and the much larger numbers that await those who seek them out.

undark.title: When Scientific Arguments Obscure Moral Ones, Democracy Suffers
undark.description: The Pentagon’s new vaccine policy values individual choice over public health. Which of these values should be prioritized is a legitimate subject for democratic debate. But when experts respond to moral arguments animating policy decisions by reiterating facts, it undermines debate and fuels divisiveness.

proj-syn.title: Nigeria’s Perilous French Gambit
proj-syn.description: Nigeria’s increasingly close relationship with France marks a departure from six decades of foreign policy aimed at reducing French influence in West Africa. An increasingly close relationship with a power that has long sought to undermine Nigerian influence in West Africa will benefit only politically connected business elites.

proj-syn.title: Autocracy Is Fueling Mexico’s Fiscal Deterioration
proj-syn.description: Mexico’s recent ratings downgrades are merely a symptom of a more serious malady: the ruling Morena party’s efforts to consolidate power permanently. To ensure the legal predictability foreign investors require, President Claudia Sheinbaum would need to confront Morena’s ideological legacy and, more importantly, its cartel ties.

proj-syn.title: The Trump Economy Is Bad News for Republicans
proj-syn.description: Donald Trump triumphed in the 2024 election by continually hammering on the Biden administration’s dismal inflation record. If his party gets shellacked in this year’s midterm elections, it will be because he has made Americans even worse off.

proj-syn.title: SpaceX Is the New East India Company
proj-syn.description: Although SpaceX is not about to rule over foreign subjects, as the chartered companies founded in the early modern era did, it, too, is operating beyond the reach of any sovereign. And like its predecessors, it has already accumulated immense powers that governments will struggle to reclaim.

proj-syn.title: The ECB Should Not Raise Interest Rates Yet
proj-syn.description: Against a backdrop of acute uncertainty, weak growth, subdued wages, and elevated market interest rates, monetary tightening is warranted only when there is convincing evidence that higher inflation is becoming entrenched. No such evidence has yet materialized in Europe.

proj-syn.title: When Markets Run on Empty
proj-syn.description: Markets are flying high despite geopolitical turmoil because a broad-based willingness to keep spending has been matched by an ability to keep doing so. But as more economic participants exhaust their means and rely on debt, a painful moment of truth will arrive—sooner rather than later if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

proj-syn.title: The Pope and the AI Profiteers
proj-syn.description: In his first encyclical, Pope Leo XIV rightly rejects the idea that markets alone can be trusted to shape society’s technological future. Recognizing that AI raises questions that prices and profits cannot answer, the Chicago-born pope has posed a direct challenge to Chicago School economics.

proj-syn.title: AI Must Not Encroach on Human Dignity
proj-syn.description: In a world captivated by technological advances, Pope Leo XIV’s first encyclical seeks to shift attention away from the marvels and terrors of AI and toward the magnificence of humanity. The message that the technology lacks a “moral conscience” and is distinct from human cognition is necessary and welcome.

proj-syn.title: The Key Forces Now Shaping Markets and Geopolitics
proj-syn.description: Three major factors are likely to shape economic and geopolitical outcomes over the next several years: politically unconstrained AI development, a shift from the logic of globalization to zero-sum thinking, and heightened international tail risks. Much could go right, or at least as expected—until it doesn’t.

proj-syn.title: The Living Ghosts of Violent Radicalism
proj-syn.description: Following World War II, the most militant student movements emerged in the former Axis powers as a way to cope with previous generations' complicity. But while the Red Army Faction and others were haunted by memories of past crimes, today's young people have mostly forgotten, and a growing number think far-right politics are cool.

proj-syn.title: Using AI to Test Policy Language
proj-syn.description: Policymakers have long understood that language affects economic behavior, but until recently, there were few tools capable of systematically analyzing its effects. AI may now help close that gap, enabling officials to anticipate how framing and timing can move markets and shift public opinion.

proj-syn.title: Europe’s Competitiveness Bogeyman
proj-syn.description: Calls for European leaders to protect domestic industry from "unfairly" subsidized Chinese competition have lately grown louder. But while tariffs might offer temporary relief to a few sectors, they cannot restore Europe's technological leadership, industrial dynamism, or export competitiveness.

proj-syn.title: Putting American Science on a MAGA Leash
proj-syn.description: A draft rule from US President Donald Trump’s White House Office of Management and Budget would subject all scientific research funding to the whims of political appointees, further undercutting a pillar of American power. The goal is to foreclose any future that is plural, contestable, and beyond the president’s control.

proj-syn.title: How Measles Came Roaring Back
proj-syn.description: Bangladesh is facing soaring measles cases not because of a single localized failure, but because of years of systemic erosion. Ultimately, maintaining herd immunity against highly contagious viruses requires relentless attention to supply and demand, as well as to the broader social and institutional foundations of public health.

proj-syn.title: Pete Hegseth’s Dangerous Call to Arms in Asia
proj-syn.description: Much like it did in Europe, the Trump administration has called on US allies in the Indo-Pacific to increase military spending to 3.5% of GDP. But a defense buildup on this scale would jeopardize economic growth and regional unity, and could lead Southeast Asian countries to gravitate toward China’s strategic orbit.

proj-syn.title: The Pope’s AI Vision and Its Limits
proj-syn.description: Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on AI is clear-eyed about the limits of techno-utopianism. But its vision of technology directed toward human flourishing needs to be extended to include the interests of every sentient being, human and nonhuman, biological or—possibly—artificial.

proj-syn.title: The Iran War Is Fueling a Global Debt Shock
proj-syn.description: Once again, a global crisis is disproportionately burdening countries that did not cause it. Across the Global South, the food- and energy-price shock triggered by the conflict in the Middle East has morphed into a debt shock that demands an urgent international response.

proj-syn.title: Democracy vs. Data Centers
proj-syn.description: As tech companies race to build data centers, communities and lawmakers across the United States are pushing back. Industry leaders frame local opposition as a threat to American competitiveness, but China’s experience shows that unchecked expansion carries serious risks of its own.
